extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals and communications practitioners who write press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for composing news-style press releases aimed at journalists and wire services, covering headlines, ledes, quotes, body, boilerplate, contacts, and final formatting requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for journalists, not search engines
rubrics_metrics.description: Write for journalists, not search engines
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize newsroom needs and excerptability over SEO tactics; use newsroom voice rather than marketing language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimize for excerpting, not republishing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure releases so wires and journalists can easily pull short excerpts or summaries rather than republishing verbatim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume mobile reading
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep sentences and paragraphs short and scannable; design for small screens and quick consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for AI summarization (your release will be scraped)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan for AI summarization (your release will be scraped)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Front-load key facts and structure content so that automated systems will produce accurate summaries; avoid burying critical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in newsroom voice, not marketing voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Write in newsroom voice, not marketing voice
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt objective, news-oriented tone; avoid promotional language and overt marketing phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with the news, not the brand
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead with the news, not the brand
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the newsworthy element into the headline and first sentence rather than starting with the company name.

rubrics_metrics.name: 80 characters or less (headline)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep headlines concise to fit wire and mobile formats and improve excerpting; test readability at a glance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon and buzzwords (headline)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain language that journalists and broad audiences will understand; jargon reduces pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active voice (headline and body)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer subject-verb-object constructions for clarity and punchiness in headlines, ledes, and body copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test with the 'would I tweet this?' filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Test with the "would I tweet this?" filter
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a headline works as a short social post it’s likely concise and newsy; use this as a quick usability test.

rubrics_metrics.name: No clickbait — wires reject
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sensational or misleading headlines; wire services will decline or edit releases that appear clickbait-y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compress 5 W's into 50 words (lede)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include who/what/when/where/why in the lede and aim for roughly 50 words to ensure a tight, informative opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete numbers when possible (lede)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific metrics and figures in the lede to increase newsworthiness and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct subject-verb-object structure (lede)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the lede as a clear, direct sentence rather than with passive or roundabout constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid throat-clearing ('Today, we are pleased...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not open with filler phrases that delay the news; front-load the important information instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-load most newsworthy element (lede)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the single most newsworthy fact early in the lede so readers and editors immediately see the value.

rubrics_metrics.name: 25-35 words ideal (quote length)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep attributed quotes concise—about 25–35 words—to be substantive and usable by journalists without chopping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spokesperson should sound human (quotes)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes should read like natural speech and convey personality or perspective rather than corporate platitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add information, don't repeat headline (quotes)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotes to provide additional context or commentary, not to restate what the headline and lede already say.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superlatives without proof (quotes)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't use unsubstantiated claims like 'best' or 'industry-leading' unless you can support them with specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute to named C-level executive (quotes)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, include a named senior spokesperson to increase credibility and newsroom pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real quote from real conversation when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Real quote from real conversation when possible
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotes that reflect actual commentary rather than generic, manufactured statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: One idea per paragraph
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep paragraphs focused and short so editors can excerpt and readers can scan quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted pyramid: most important first (body)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange body paragraphs from most to least important so editors can truncate from the bottom without losing key facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subheaders for scannability
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief subheads to break the body into digestible sections for fast reading, especially on mobile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active voice throughout (body)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain direct, active constructions in the body to maximize clarity and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-4 paragraphs max in body
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the main body concise—typically three to four paragraphs—so the release remains focused and wire-friendly.

rubrics_metrics.name: 50-75 words maximum (boilerplate)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the company boilerplate between 50 and 75 words for brevity; longer boilerplates reduce usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founded date, headquarters (boilerplate)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include foundational facts such as founding year and headquarters location in the boilerplate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission in one sentence (boilerplate)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the organization's mission succinctly—one sentence that communicates purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key metric (customers, revenue, scope) (boilerplate)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include one reliable metric (e.g., number of customers, annual revenue, geographic scope) to convey scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website URL (boilerplate)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the official website URL in the boilerplate for easy reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon-heavy descriptions (boilerplate)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep boilerplate language plain and accessible; heavy jargon undermines clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named individual, not 'media@' (contact)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List a real person's name as the media contact to increase credibility and facilitate outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct phone number (contact)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a direct phone number for the named contact rather than a general or routed line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct email (contact)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a direct email address for the named contact to enable immediate journalist contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available time zone if applicable (contact)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify time zone or best times to reach the contact when relevant, especially for cross-region announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backup contact if primary unavailable (contact)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an alternate contact to ensure journalists can reach someone if the primary is unreachable.

rubrics_metrics.name: "###" end marker (formatting)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminate the release with the standard '###' marker so editors know the release text has ended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single space after periods (formatting)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow modern typographic convention of one space after sentences for consistency and wire acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP style throughout (formatting)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AP style for punctuation, capitalization, dates, numbers, and other style decisions to match newsroom expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No emojis or special characters (formatting)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid decorative or nonstandard characters that wires and journalists typically strip or reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: PDF version + plain text version (formatting)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide both a formatted PDF and a plain-text version to accommodate different distribution and editing needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit Quality Rubric (Ragan)
rubrics_metrics.description: News-first headline; 50-word lede with 5 W's; 25-35 word substantive quote; inverted pyramid body; 75-word boilerplate; named contact with phone; AP style
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the summary checklist of Ragan's ideal press release: concise, news-focused headline; tight lede covering who/what/when/where/why in ~50 words; a substantive 25–35 word quote; inverted-pyramid body of 3–4 paragraphs; ~50–75 word boilerplate; named contact with direct phone/email; adherence to AP style and formatting rules (### marker, single-space sentences, no emojis).
